Tinder Scams UK: How to Spot a Fake Profile or Romance Con

Tinder scams can cost you thousands — here's how to spot them before you lose money.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-04-21 · Updated 2026-07-26 · 10 min read

Tinder scamTinder romance scamfake Tinder profile
Quick answer: Tinder requires Face Check for new UK users from 26 March 2026, but a Photo Verified badge shows only that a live face matched the profile photos—not that every claim is honest. Keep early conversations in Tinder, never use a verification link sent by a match, and treat requests for money or investment pitches as scams.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

Three high-risk decision points on Tinder

Three moments on Tinder carry most of the financial risk, and each has a clean decision attached to it.

  • A new match asks you to prove you are real by using a link they send you. Decision: never open it. A match cannot issue or complete Tinder verification for you.
  • A match wants your number in the first handful of exchanges. Decision: slow down. That is a red flag rather than conclusive proof of fraud, and Tinder's own safety tips say to keep conversations on Tinder while you are getting to know someone.
  • Weeks in, a warm and attentive person mentions a trading platform they use. Decision: treat that as fraud from its first mention, however long you have been talking. Tinder's safety tips put it plainly: do not let a match talk you into investing or opening an account with a service or website they share.

None of this requires you to be suspicious of people in general. Each one is a discrete choice with a right answer, which is why it is worth settling them in advance rather than mid-conversation with someone you are enjoying.

What the Photo Verified badge actually proves

From 26 March 2026 Tinder began rolling Face Check out to new UK users, and describes it as required for all new UK users. You record a short video selfie in the app; Tinder's system tests that a real, physically present person took it and compares the face with the profile photos, then awards the Photo Verified badge. In earlier Face Check markets Tinder reported more than a 60 per cent fall in exposure to potential bad actors and more than a 40 per cent fall in bad-actor reports — those are Tinder's own measured results.

Separately, Tinder offers an optional ID + Photo Verification process, which checks a government-issued ID against a selfie and profile likeness and confirms age; Tinder says expressly that it does not guarantee the ID's validity or a user's safety.

Read the badge for exactly what it is. The badge shows that Tinder's liveness and face-matching checks succeeded. Tinder also uses Face Check to detect the same face across multiple accounts, but neither the badge nor that detection guarantees a person's name, biography, location, relationship status or intentions.

The mandatory Face Check announcement applies to new users, so an older account should not be assumed to have completed it.

Face Check is a floor, not a character reference. Tinder's safety tips suggest a phone or video call as a screening step before meeting, and somebody who keeps producing reasons never to take one has told you something the badge cannot. Note, though, that Tinder's in-app Face to Face video chat has been discontinued, so any such call will run on a separate service. Arrange it if you want to, and carry on talking in Tinder afterwards rather than abandoning the in-app record.

The 'get yourself verified first' link is always a scam

One pattern is close to universal on Tinder. An enthusiastic new match explains that she only meets people who are safety-verified, then sends a link to a site with a name in the style of safe-dating-verify.com or datesafe-id.net. The page imitates a background-check service. It wants your name, date of birth, email address and card number, and promises the card is only there to confirm you are an adult.

An unsolicited verification page like that may steal personal or payment information, and nothing on the page tells you which. There is no upside to filling it in.

The rule to hold on to is narrow and it is reliable. A match cannot issue or complete Tinder verification for you. Never use a verification link sent by a match. Start any genuine account or age-verification process only from Tinder's own app, site or help flow.

It is worded that way on purpose, because Tinder itself can send you outwards: an account restricted on age grounds may be directed from an in-app prompt to a third-party age-verification service. What matters is where the journey starts. A link that arrives in a chat is not a Tinder flow, and the response is to report the account rather than reason with it. If the same lure reaches you by email, forward it to report@phishing.gov.uk.

Tinder's safety prompts, and what they do not tell you

Several Tinder features fire on their own. Read them as safety prompts, which is what Tinder calls them — not as findings about the person you are talking to.

  • Contact Exchange Alerts appear when Tinder detects contact details being shared in a chat. The prompt surfaces safety information; it does not mean the app has judged the timing, or the person, abnormal.
  • Are You Sure? asks a sender to reconsider a message that looks inappropriate, and Does This Bother You? offers the person receiving it an immediate route to report.
  • Photo Verified Chat, when you enable it, restricts incoming messages to Photo Verified members. Tinder does not claim it removes any particular share of throwaway or bot accounts.
  • Block Contacts lets you pre-block people from your phone's contact list. It is best-effort by Tinder's own account: Tinder says it cannot prevent two people seeing each other if the uploaded contact details do not match the details used to create the account.

None of these stops a patient, funded operator. What they do is interrupt you for a second, which is the only thing a prompt can do — the decision still belongs to you.

When Telegram and a trading app enter the conversation

The most expensive Tinder pattern is not the urgent-emergency story. It is the slow one, where there is no crisis, no request and nothing to refuse. Across several weeks a match becomes a fixture of your day, mentions in passing that an uncle or a mentor handles money for the family, and eventually shares an app or web platform with a tidy interface and a balance that ticks upward.

A small opening deposit appears to grow. That screen is fabricated. Attempt a withdrawal and a charge appears: tax, a compliance fee, an account-upgrade minimum, an unlocking payment. Every one of those is another deposit into the same fraud, and paying one always reveals another.

Two details are specific to how this reaches you through Tinder. First, the chat usually leaves the app early, for WhatsApp or Telegram. Tinder holds the messages that remain in its own service and cannot review a conversation on another platform at all, so moving off-platform takes everything that follows out of Tinder's in-app moderation view unless you preserve it and supply it yourself.

Second, check the named platform on the FCA Firm Checker at register.fca.org.uk before any money moves, not afterwards. Look the firm up, read what it is actually authorised to do, and confirm that every contact detail you have been given matches the register. A fraudulent platform may be missing from the register altogether — but a scammer may equally impersonate an authorised firm or quote a genuine firm's real details, so a name that does appear is not a clean bill of health. Start the check from the FCA's own page, never from a link the match supplies.

To pressure-test the site itself, our guide at Is This Website a Scam? A Practical Checklist Before You Buy walks through the checks.

Screenshot first, then unmatch, block and report

Order matters. Capture screenshots first: the profile, the photos, the whole chat, any usernames, numbers, links or wallet addresses. The moment you unmatch, the conversation disappears from your side of the app.

Then open the three-dot menu on the profile or in the chat and choose to report — there is also a report button at the foot of every profile you can see. Follow the on-screen prompts, pick a reason, and add the details that help. Who submitted a report and what it said stay confidential, but Tinder does say a reported person may receive a generic notification that a report led to their account being reviewed, so do not assume nobody is told anything. Blocking removes their profile from your feed and stops them contacting you again.

If you unmatched first and only later realised what was happening, you have not lost the chance. Tinder's Safety Center carries an online route for reporting someone you unmatched, or who unmatched you, so the report is still possible once the connection is gone. Make it anyway: yours may be the report that closes an account currently working through dozens of other people.

If you have already paid

Being targeted says nothing bad about your judgement. These are staffed, scripted operations run at industrial scale, working through many people at once with material that has been tested on other targets before it reached you.

Work in this order.

  • Ring your bank today and use the phrase authorised push payment fraud. Money sent by Faster Payments or CHAPS from a UK account on or after 7 October 2024 may be reimbursable under the rules currently in force, to a maximum of £85,000, with a possible excess of up to £100 and a 13-month window to claim. Every case is assessed individually, so treat this as a claim worth making rather than a refund to expect.
  • Card payments run on a separate track: ask your issuer about disputing the transaction.
  • Ask Cifas about Protective Registration if you handed over identity documents or personal details.
  • Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In Scotland, call Police Scotland on 101.

Our /recovery/ checklist sets out the full sequence, including what to preserve as evidence and who to tell in what order.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Photo Verified badge mean my Tinder match is genuine?

It means Tinder's liveness and face-matching checks succeeded — a live person recorded a selfie that matched the profile photos. It guarantees nothing about their name, biography, location, relationship status or intentions. Tinder says Face Check is required for new UK users from 26 March 2026, so the badge is now ordinary rather than remarkable.

A match sent a link to get me 'safety verified' before we meet. Is it real?

No. A match cannot issue or complete Tinder verification for you, so a verification link that arrives in a chat is never legitimate. The page may steal personal or payment information. Start any genuine account or age-verification process only from Tinder's own app, site or help flow, and report the account instead of replying.

Tinder showed a safety warning when we swapped numbers. Should I worry?

That is Contact Exchange Alerts working as designed. It is a safety prompt triggered by contact details being shared, not a judgement about the timing or the person, so it is not an accusation and not evidence. Use the pause it gives you: Tinder's own tips suggest staying in the app while you get to know someone.

I unmatched before I thought about reporting. Is it too late?

No. Tinder's Safety Center has an online route covering someone you unmatched, or who unmatched you, so a report is still possible. Whatever you screenshotted beforehand will make it far more useful to their moderators.

My match steered me into a trading app and now I cannot withdraw. What now?

Stop paying. Withdrawal taxes, release charges and upgrade minimums are all part of the same fraud. Phone your bank the same day, look the platform up on the FCA Firm Checker starting from the FCA's own site, and report it. Recovery is uncertain, particularly with cryptocurrency, but speed genuinely improves the odds.
